summary.text: A false vacuum is a hypothetical vacuum state in quantum field theory that is locally stable but not the most stable possible ground state.
It could last a very long time but might eventually decay into the more stable vacuum, most commonly imagined as a small bubble of that vacuum forming by chance and spreading.
If our universe is in a false vacuum, the decay could range from subtle changes in some cosmological parameters to the end of existing forces and particles.

items.prompt: A ball rests in a small dip on a hillside, with a deeper valley further down. Which vacuum idea does the dip match?

options.label: A true vacuum, at a global minimum of energy
A false vacuum, at a local minimum of energy
A vacuum with no quantum fields at all
A vacuum with the highest possible energy

items.explain: A false vacuum is a local minimum of energy, while a true vacuum sits at the global minimum.

items.prompt: A false vacuum is called metastable. What does that say about it?

options.label: It is perfectly stable and can never change
It decays almost immediately after forming
It may last a very long time but could eventually decay
It exists only where there are no quantum fields

items.explain: A false vacuum may last a very long time but could eventually decay to the more stable one.

items.prompt: Somewhere in space, a tiny region by chance falls into a more stable vacuum and the change spreads outward. What is this process called?

options.label: Bubble nucleation
Quantum folding
Field collapse
Bubble inflation

items.explain: The most common suggestion for how vacuum decay might happen is bubble nucleation, where a small region reaches a more stable vacuum and spreads.

items.prompt: Does gravity make a false vacuum more likely to decay?

options.label: Yes, it always speeds up the decay
Yes, but only inside the bubble
No, it has no effect on decay at all
No, it generally makes decay less likely

items.explain: In general, gravitation makes the probability of vacuum decay smaller, and it can even prevent decay altogether.

items.prompt: Why might we underestimate the chance of being destroyed by vacuum decay?

options.label: Its warning signs fade before they reach Earth
News of it would reach us only as we were destroyed
Telescopes cannot look at the right region of sky
Its frequency is already measured and found to be zero

items.explain: Because of observer selection effects, any information about vacuum decay would reach us only at the instant we were destroyed, unlike impacts or supernovae whose frequencies we can measure.

items.prompt: Would every false vacuum decay destroy everything in the universe?

options.label: Yes, every scenario ends all matter at once
Yes, but only life on planets would be lost
No, some scenarios leave galaxies, stars and life surviving
No, every scenario changes only distant space

items.explain: Some decay scenarios are compatible with the survival of galaxies, stars and even life, while others involve full destruction of baryonic matter.

paragraphs.heading: A vacuum that is not the lowest
paragraphs.text: In quantum field theory, a vacuum is a space holding as little energy as it can, yet it is not truly empty: quantum fields are still present. A false vacuum is a proposed vacuum state that sits at a local minimum of energy rather than the lowest possible one. Physicists call such a state metastable. A true vacuum, by contrast, sits at the global minimum of energy and so is fully stable.

paragraphs.heading: How it could decay
paragraphs.text: A false vacuum might hold steady for an extremely long time, but it could in the end drop into the more stable state. That change is called false vacuum decay. The most common picture of how it might happen in our universe is bubble nucleation. If some small patch of space happened by chance to reach the more stable vacuum, that bubble would spread outward.

paragraphs.heading: Could our universe be one
paragraphs.text: The vacuum we live in is usually assumed to be a true vacuum. But it is possible that it is instead a local minimum and not the global one, which would make it false. If so, a decay to the true vacuum could have dramatic results. Depending mostly on the energy gap between the two states, the effects could range from a subtle shift in some cosmological parameters to the end of today's fundamental forces and particles. Some versions would let galaxies, stars and even life survive, while others involve the complete destruction of baryonic matter or an immediate gravitational collapse of the universe.

paragraphs.heading: What gravity does
paragraphs.text: Gravity generally makes vacuum decay less likely. For decay to happen, it must be possible to build a bubble whose total energy is zero. Without gravity this always works, however small the energy difference, as long as the bubble is made large enough. With gravity, the true vacuum's negative energy density distorts the geometry inside the bubble, and when the energy difference is small enough, no bubble has a large enough ratio of volume to surface. In that extreme case gravity can even keep the false vacuum stable and stop decay altogether.

paragraphs.heading: A risk we cannot see coming
paragraphs.text: In a 2005 paper in Nature, Max Tegmark and Nick Bostrom put the risk of Earth being destroyed by all natural events, a shift to a lower vacuum state included, at less than 1/10⁹ per year. They noted a catch, which they traced to observer selection effects. News of a vacuum decay would reach us only at the moment it destroyed us, so we might underestimate how likely it is. Risks such as impacts, gamma-ray bursts and supernovae are different, because we have direct measures of how often they happen.

paragraphs.heading: Inflation and the Higgs
paragraphs.text: A number of theories suggest that cosmic inflation may come from a false vacuum decaying into the true one. Alan Guth's original inflation proposal had inflation end through bubble nucleation. It was soon understood that such violent tunneling could not keep the universe the same everywhere and in every direction, so Andrei Linde, and separately Andreas Albrecht and Paul Steinhardt, proposed slow roll inflation with no tunneling. Since the top quark was found in 1995 and the Higgs boson in 2012, the electroweak interaction has been seen as the most promising candidate for a metastable force. This version of the idea is called electroweak or Higgs vacuum instability.
